title: Analytic Bijections for Smooth and Interpretable Normalizing Flows
claim: Different bijection families reshape a base density in distinct ways: local deformation, global shift, or uniform scaling, with differing expressivity.
layout: 2x3 grid; transform curves on top, resulting densities below, shared legend
description: A 2×3 grid of small line plots comparing three scalar bijections, with columns titled Cubic Rational, Sinh and Affine Linear. The top row plots y against x. The blue h(x) curve is drawn over a dashed gray identity line. Cubic rational bends sharply near the origin and then rejoins the identity. Sinh has a gentler S-shaped bend and stays offset from the identity at large |x|. Affine is a straight line with a different slope. A shared legend sits in the middle: identity, h(x), prior and transformed. The bottom row plots density against x. A dotted black Gaussian prior is overlaid with an orange transformed density. Cubic rational gives two sharp narrow peaks. Sinh gives a smooth bimodal shape. Affine gives a slightly wider Gaussian. Blue and orange are the main colors. The eye goes first to the sharp orange peaks in the bottom-left panel.
caption: Three bijection behaviors. Left: Local deformation (cubic rational) creates bimodal structure while h(x) →x for large |x|. Middle: Global shift (sinh) displaces distant points by constant offset. Right: Uniform scaling (affine, for comparison).
abstract: A key challenge in normalizing flows is finding expressive invertible scalar bijections. Existing approaches face trade-offs: affine transformations are smooth and analytically invertible but lack expressivity; monotonic splines offer local control but are only piecewise smooth and act on bounded domains; residual flows achieve smoothness but need numerical inversion. We introduce three families of analytic bijections that are globally smooth ($C^\infty$), defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$, and analytically invertible in closed form, combining the favorable properties of prior approaches. Beyond serving as drop-in replacements in coupling flows, where they match or exceed spline performance, we develop radial flows: a novel architecture using direct parametrization that transforms the radial coordinate while preserving angular direction. Radial flows exhibit exceptional training stability, produce geometrically interpretable transformations, and on targets with radial structure can achieve comparable quality to coupling flows with $1000\times$ fewer parameters. We provide comprehensive evaluation on 1D and 2D benchmarks, and demonstrate applicability to higher-dimensional physics problems through experiments on $Ï^4$ lattice field theory, where our bijections outperform affine baselines and enable problem-specific designs that address mode collapse.
